idiom_name: opaque struct (incomplete type in the header) + pointer-only API
implementation_notes: C has no classes and no copy operations to delete, so the mixin is replaced by information hiding at the translation-unit boundary: declare an incomplete type in the public header (`typedef struct Conn Conn;`) and define the struct only in the implementation file. A by-value copy or a `sizeof` of an incomplete type is a compile error ('invalid use of undefined type', storage size unknown), and every operation takes a pointer, so a client cannot manufacture a second object or inspect the representation; ownership is moved by handing the pointer over and released through one destroy function. The classic base-class form is not expressible; the residual risk is that once the definition is visible (a private header included by callers, or a deliberate fixed-size handle), C lets `memcpy` duplicate the bytes, so the guarantee is only as strong as header hygiene.
pitfalls: The guarantee depends on the definition staying private: if callers can see `struct Conn` (or a fixed-size `unsigned char data[N]` handle), `memcpy` is legal and silently duplicates the resource.
Pointers are copyable and C copies them implicitly, so two owners can alias one resource - the C analogue of a bad copy; document the single owner and keep one destroy path.
By-value APIs cannot even be declared against an incomplete type, so this idiom rules out small inline values and value-returning getters; use a visible struct plus immutability for those.
